items_missed: No agenda statement with a timeframe and no 'sound good?' confirmation. The closest thing was 'let's chat about a bit. Well a couple of questions and then the next step will be like a virtual walkthrough of the actual office itself' — a roadmap she contradicted one turn later with 'I honestly don't think more we'll need the virtual walkthrough.' The customer never knew how long the call would take or that pricing was coming.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. The call opened straight into 'This is Jessa with Einstein Moving Company. How can I help you?'

Never asked for the customer's name — Shannon volunteered it ('My name is Shannon. I'm calling from credit central'). No last name captured either; the spelling only surfaced accidentally from the email address ('S. Montrose M-O-N-T R-O-S-E').

Zero pricing delivered on the call. No 'pricing is super simple' opener, no hourly rate per mover, no what's-included list (gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools), no 'no hidden fees' pitch. The entire value block was deferred: 'what I'm gonna do next is work up the actual estimate for you that will take me maybe like 10 15 minutes or so and I will email it over to you.'

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — the biggest miss on this call, because the customer teed it up directly with 'does your company carry workers comp and general liability insurance?' The answer was 'We do yes' plus a COI offer, and nothing about the $2,000 accidental-damage coverage or the 60¢/lb baseline.

No clock explanation at all — no 'clock starts on-site when the contract opens,' no 2.5-hour minimum, no 15-minute prorated increments, no sense-check. On an hourly commercial job with ten filing cabinets and roughly fifteen chairs, the customer has no idea how the bill is built.

Disassembly/reassembly never raised despite four desks, ten filing cabinets and a printer stand — desks are the single most likely disassembly item on an office move and it was never priced, timed, or even asked about.

No estimate framing of any kind: no typical time range for a 1,000 sq ft office, no crew size, no truck count. She gathered the 50-foot walk distance ('would you say like fairly close within like fifty feet or so') but never explained it back as a variable that moves the number.

Entire Save Your Ass section absent. The customer handed her the opening — 'if it's stuff that small like, their what's in their desk and stuff they would probably just put it in a box and move it ourselves honestly' — and the reply was just 'Okay. Gotcha, okay.' No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no carload tip, no sense-check.

No booking attempt. She confirmed live availability ('I'm looking at those days, twenty fourth, twenty fifth of this month... Looks like we do awesome') and then never asked for the date. No 'want to go ahead and lock that in?'
No 'no deposit required' — a genuine differentiator for a business customer routing an expense, and it went unsaid.

Email handoff explained but not to standard: no BOLDED key details at the top of the email, and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. The only follow-up framing was 'if you're left with any questions. So call me back. Email me back.'
Business hours and how to reach the team never given.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked about.
Customer's name used once ('Shannon, you'll have my email here in a little bit') — short of the 3+ standard.

Heavy verbal filler undercut authority: 'I guess' appears eight-plus times ('I guess what', 'I guess starting questions is', 'I guess probably the next best step', 'I guess for now my last question is') alongside repeated 'Gotcha. Gotcha. Okay.' stacks.
top_strength: The discovery was genuinely good — this is a well-run intake on an unusual call type. Jespah handled a commercial inbound she had no script for and built a usable inventory picture: she checked the date first and confirmed availability live, pulled both zips ('From seven eight two five one and two seven eight two two seven'), got square footage, room count, floor level at both ends, time-of-day building restrictions, and pinned down truck access with a concrete number rather than a vague answer — 'would you say like fairly close within like fifty feet or so fifty feet or less?' She then worked the inventory patiently, catching items the customer hadn't volunteered by prompting 'anything else being moved that you can think of even like things on the walls or floors like artwork or runs' and 'I'm assuming with the poor desk, we'll have, I'm assuming the four desk chairs' — which is what surfaced the roughly fifteen chairs. She also read the walkthrough threshold correctly and saved the customer a step: 'for something that size we might, I honestly don't think more we'll need the virtual walkthrough, I think we can just chat about it here.' And she was proactive on the commercial paperwork before being asked: 'if you need that like in a, like an actual COI sent over to you like certificate we can do that as well.' She stayed easy when the customer put her on hold to go count desks — 'Oh, sure. That's fine. No rush here.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: she gathered everything and sold nothing. This was a nine-and-a-half minute call where the customer's stated reason for calling was 'I'm just trying to see if I can get a quote for a move, please' — and he hung up without hearing a rate, what's included, the clock structure, or a single differentiator. All of it got pushed into an email he may or may not read. Before asking for the email address she needed a live value block: 'Shannon, before I put the estimate together, let me tell you how our pricing works because it's super simple — it's a flat hourly rate per mover, and that covers the truck, gas, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands and tools, plus disassembling and reassembling those desks. The clock starts on-site when we open the contract, there's a two-and-a-half hour minimum, and after that we bill in fifteen-minute increments. No credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees, and no deposit to hold the twenty-fourth. Does that make sense?' Second priority, and it was a layup: he asked point-blank about insurance and got 'We do yes.' The line was 'We do — general liability and workers comp, and I'll send the COI. On top of that every move includes our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to two thousand dollars per move to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, which matters here with ten filing cabinets and computer equipment moving.' Third: she confirmed the 24th and 25th were open and then never asked for the business. On a job this clean the close is 'I can pencil you in for Thursday the twenty-fourth right now with no deposit, and the estimate will be in your inbox in fifteen minutes — if the numbers don't work you just reply and we release it.' One process note for Amanda: this is a commercial office move being graded against a residential scorecard, and several deductions (Save Your Ass consolidation examples, Ecobox, home size in bedrooms) map awkwardly. The differentiator and clock deductions are real and would apply on any call. Open commitments to verify got logged: a generic COI plus W9 promised with the estimate, and an emailed estimate promised within 10-15 minutes of a 3:58pm call. Also worth a quick fix — 'This is Jessa' when the roster name is Jespah is fine as a preferred name, but the estimate email needs to match whichever name she gives on the phone.
phone_presence_notes: Patient, agreeable and easy to talk to — 'Yeah, sure. Absolutely' and 'Oh, sure. That's fine. No rush here' when he stepped away to count desks — but the warmth was thin and repetitive, with 'Gotcha. Gotcha. Okay.' carrying most of the acknowledgment, no empathy statements, no humor, and the name used only once.
audio_review_reason: Speaking clarity and pace is one of the deductions, and the transcript is garbled in exactly the stretches needed to judge it — 'SM refrigeration', 'how many desks and filing come to see you', 'the poor desk', 'let me pull my calendar up here to stop by' — plus heavily interleaved turns where the customer's lines land out of order. Audio confirms whether the filler and self-interruption are real delivery habits or transcription noise.
